newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Anglo Gencor mineral swap seen wise.
newsitem.headline: Anglo Gencor mineral swap seen wise.

text.p: Anglo American Corp of South Africa and Gencor Ltd's mineral rights swap was sensible as both parties would be able to access untouched ore and open up an additional 230 tonnes of gold, analysts said on Friday.

Anglogold and Gengold on Thursday jointly announced that they had agreed to swap mineral rights, thereby allowing several of their mines to gain access to reserves previously denied by existing mineral rights.

The two companies said that mines like Gengold's Beatrix Mines Ltd, Oryx Gold Holdings Ltd and Evander Gold Mines Ltd and Anglogold's Vaal Reefs Exploration and Mining Co Ltd, would be able to extend their current operations by access to contiguous ground.

"It is a win-win situation for both companies. As far as the two companies are concerned they were swapping (areas that) effectively contain the same amount of gold, so nobody wins over the next," analyst Dave Giese of stockbrokers Davis Borkum Hare said.
Analysts said that the rationalisation of mineral rights, which had been gathered since the heady days of South Africa's gold rush more than a century ago, amounted to good business sense.

"Because of the rush of mineral rights in the good old days where everybody got what they could, without any intention of really turning it to account, the realisation has come that in order to turn it to account you have to do a deal with your neighbours," Giese said.
Mathison and Hollidge gold analyst Angus Auchterlonie agreed: "Obviously if you had sterile ore reserves that you can turn to account, it is good news".
Although AngloGold and Gengold only announced the deal on Thursday, agreement had been reached some time ago, James Capel Simpson Mckie gold analyst Simon Village said.

"It is really no great shakes, the deal really took place a long time ago," Village said, adding that Anglogold's Vaal Reefs had been mining Weltevrede Mines Ltd -- of which Gengold held 76.6 percent, until Thursday -- for some time.

"I think what they have really done is tied up the other loose ends about the other properties. As far as we are concerned it really amounts to little more than good housekeeping as far as mineral rights are concerned," he said.
He said Anglo and Gencor had now embarked on a more rational approach to mineral rights.

"What we are also finding is a greater willingness to trade mineral rights on the perceived value of the gold that is there. In the past, uncertainty, rightly or wrongly, as to how much gold was there might have been a reason for them to say 'I am not prepared to swap you this ground for that ground because I think I've got more gold than you've got'," Village said.
"There is a more pragmatic approach now where efficiencies are more important," Village added.
The mine that stood to gain the most from the rationalisation was Vaal Reefs, analysts said.

Bobby Godsell, Anglogold's chief operating officer, has said Vaal Reefs would have access to an additional 115 tonnes (3.7 million ounces of gold), which the mine should be able to exploit within the immediate future without significant additional infrastructure.

Among the benefits for Gengold was the potential addition of about two million resource ounces to its Beatrix mine -- the lowest cost producer in the South African industry, which is burdened by falling grades and increasing working costs.
Gengold managing director Tom Dale said the deal held several benefits for primary stakeholders in the industry.
"I compliment industry leaders who are actively pursuing commercially logical mineral rights exchange," he said.
